overall.summary: Every stated number reproduces and nothing is refuted. findings.statement: read as a whole, the layer makes the network depend on the bottom row and the lower centre squares, and hardly on the upper rows
findings.check: holding a square at its average tests the whole model and is weighted by how often the square is filled; compared with the layer's per-piece weights
findings.evidence: Every square reaches the output only through this layer, so the AUC test is a whole-model property. Per piece, the layer reacts more to the upper squares: sum |w|/sd per square is 61 to 222 in row 6 and 19 to 31 in row 1. The low dependence on upper rows comes from occupancy (row 6 filled on 0 to 1% of boards, row 1 on 40 to 76%), which the hypothesis mentions, not from the layer weighting them less.

findings.statement: the left side of the bottom row (a1 to c1) matters more than the right side (e1 to f1); "this is Connect-4 square value"
findings.check: mirror pairs compared
findings.evidence: reproduces (c1 0.9042 vs e1 0.9252, b1 0.9091 vs f1 0.9346; a1 0.9136 vs g1 0.9156 about equal). Connect-4 is left-right symmetric, so square value would be symmetric; the asymmetry is the model's own, not a game property.

findings.statement: self-probe: boards 9999 and 9786 with the x piece on d1 turned into o (50% -> 13%; 67% -> 71%, "units 46 and 47 turn on")
findings.check: own probe; piece counts of the training boards
findings.evidence: Values reproduce (0.4954 -> 0.1291, unit 47 4.23 -> 9.12, unit 46 0 -> 0.62; 0.6745 -> 0.7143, 39 2.25 -> 0, 46 4.25, 47 4.04). But every training board has exactly 4 x and 4 o, and the flip makes 3 x and 5 o: both cases are outside the data. On 9786 unit 46 was already on (0.12). An in-support version (swap the x on d1 with an o on another bottom square, counts kept, n = 7465) lowers the chance on 93% of boards (median -0.24), so the reading stands but the probe is weak evidence.
